1120680.overview:
### Summary

The development server contains a path traversal vulnerability on Windows when serving files from `servedir`.

Due to the use of `path.Clean()` (which only normalizes forward-slash `/` separators) instead of a Windows-aware path normalization function, it is possible to craft requests using backslashes (`\`) that bypass the intended directory containment logic. An attacker can escape the configured `servedir` root and access arbitrary files on the filesystem.
This issue affects Windows environments only.

### Details

The request path is sanitized using:
```go
// https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/blob/v0.27.3/pkg/api/serve_other.go#L165
queryPath := path.Clean(req.URL.Path)[1:]
```


However:
- `path.Clean()` is POSIX-style and only understands `/` (docs: `https://pkg.go.dev/path#Clean`)
- On Windows, `\` is a valid path separator
- `path.Clean()` does not treat `\` as a separator

Later, the server constructs the absolute path:
```go
// https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/blob/v0.27.3/pkg/api/serve_other.go#L221
absPath := h.fs.Join(h.servedir, queryPath)
```

If `queryPath` contains sequences such as:
```
..\..\..\..\..\..\..\Windows\system.ini
```

`path.Clean()` will not normalize them, but the Windows filesystem will interpret `\` as directory separators when resolving `absPath`.
Because the implementation does not verify that the final resolved path remains within `servedir`, it allows directory traversal outside the intended root directory.
### Vulnerable Code

```go
// https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/blob/v0.27.3/pkg/api/serve_other.go#L165
	queryPath := path.Clean(req.URL.Path)[1:]
	....
	// Check for a file in the "servedir" directory
	if h.servedir != "" && kind != fs.FileEntry {
		absPath := h.fs.Join(h.servedir, queryPath)
		if absDir := h.fs.Dir(absPath); absDir != absPath {
			if entries, err, _ := h.fs.ReadDirectory(absDir); err == nil {
				if entry, _ := entries.Get(h.fs.Base(absPath)); entry != nil && entry.Kind(h.fs) == fs.FileEntry {
	....				
```


### Steps to reproduce

```
npm install --save-exact --save-dev esbuild

echo "console.log(1)" > app.js

.\node_modules\.bin\esbuild --version
0.27.3

.\node_modules\.bin\esbuild app.js --bundle --outdir=www --servedir=www --watch

curl -i --path-as-is "http://localhost:8000/..\..\..\..\..\..\..\Windows\system.ini"
<content of Windows\system.ini>
```


### Impact

- Arbitrary file read on Windows
- Exposure of sensitive files

1241206.overview:
### Impact

KaTeX can act as a read-side prototype pollution gadget in applications where `Object.prototype` has already been polluted, or where an attacker can influence the prototype of the renderer options object. (KaTeX does not enable said prototype pollution. This advisory applies when combining KaTeX with other vulnerable software that allows for prototype pollution.)

Affected versions may treat inherited properties from `Object.prototype` as renderer options, internal setting metadata, or namespace entries. In particular, an inherited `trust` value will be treated as though the application explicitly enabled trusted rendering, rather than using the documented default of `false`.

With attacker-controlled mathematical expressions, this can produce links capable of user-interaction cross-site scripting or load attacker-selected external resources. Exploitation requires the consuming application to insert KaTeX output into a web page without a separate sanitizer. (KaTeX does not execute scripts merely by rendering an expression.)

Other inherited settings can alter rendering behavior or resource limits. Inherited setting metadata can affect how defaults and supplied options are processed, while inherited namespace properties can be mistaken for defined macros or other internal values.

### Patches

Upgrade to KaTeX v0.18.2 to remove this vulnerability.

### Workarounds

- Address any prototype-pollution vulnerability in the application or its dependencies.
- `delete Object.prototype.trust`, `delete Object.prototype.default`, and `delete Object.prototype.processor` before calling KaTeX
- Do not allow untrusted input to control the renderer options object or its prototype.
- Sanitize KaTeX-generated HTML before inserting it into a document.

### Details

KaTeX previously used ordinary JavaScript property access in the following contexts:

- Renderer settings could be inherited from the prototype of the options object.
- Internal `default` and `processor` setting metadata could be inherited from `Object.prototype`.
- Namespace lookup could treat inherited properties as built-in definitions.
- Namespace group restoration could preserve an inherited property as though it had been an explicitly defined value.

The fix adds own-property checks to each of these paths. Inherited properties are no longer accepted as renderer settings, setting metadata, namespace definitions, or values to be restored after a group ends.

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

- Open an issue or security advisory in the [KaTeX repository](https://github.com/KaTeX/KaTeX/)
- Email us at [katex-security@mit.edu](mailto:katex-security@mit.edu)
1241206.title: KaTeX: Existing prototype pollution can bypass trust restrictions

1241247.overview:
### Impact

Multiple `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-*` packages recorded the database connection username as the `db.user`
span attribute on every instrumented database operation. This attribute was emitted unconditionally — it was
not gated by `enhancedDatabaseReporting` or any other opt-in flag, and it was the **default** behaviour for
all users of the affected packages until the patched releases shipped on 2026-07-23.

The attribute is forwarded to every configured observability backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Datadog, OTLP
collectors, etc.).  Depending on the database account naming convention in use, the exported value may
reveal:

- Internal service account names that disclose architecture topology.
- Role-encoded usernames (e.g. `admin_readwrite`, `app_readonly_prod`) useful for privilege inference.
- Database account naming patterns useful for credential enumeration.

Affected packages (all are vulnerable from the first published version through the version listed below):

| Package | Vulnerable range | Patched version |
|---------|-----------------|-----------------|
| `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-cassandra-driver` | `< 0.66.0` | `0.66.0` |
| `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-knex`             | `< 0.65.0` | `0.65.0` |
| `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-mongoose`         | `< 0.67.0` | `0.67.0` |
| `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-mysql`            | `< 0.67.0` | `0.67.0` |
| `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-mysql2`           | `< 0.67.0` | `0.67.0` |
| `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-oracledb`         | `< 0.46.0` | `0.46.0` |
| `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-pg`               | `< 0.73.0` | `0.73.0` |
| `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-tedious`          | `< 0.40.0` | `0.40.0` |

### Patches

Fixed in the coordinated release on 2026-07-23 via
[feat!: only emit stable http, network and database attributes (#3585)](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-js-contrib/pull/3585).

Upgrade to the patched version listed in the table above for each instrumentation package in use.

### Workarounds

No configuration-level workaround exists in the affected versions: the `db.user` attribute cannot be
suppressed without patching. As a partial mitigation, a custom `SpanProcessor` can be used to strip `db.user` from spans before they leave the process:

```ts
// Example: drop db.user in a custom SpanProcessor
class StripDbUserProcessor implements SpanProcessor {
  onStart(span: Span) {
    span.setAttribute('db.user', null);
  }
  onEnd() {}
  shutdown() { return Promise.resolve(); }
  forceFlush() { return Promise.resolve(); }
}
```

Users who control the downstream collector can also filter the attribute at the collector pipeline level.
1241247.title: Multiple @opentelemetry/instrumentation-* packages expose database username via unconditional db.user span attribute

```ts
class StripDbUserProcessor implements SpanProcessor {
  onStart(span: Span) {
    span.setAttribute('db.user', null);
  }
  onEnd() {}
  shutdown() { return Promise.resolve(); }
  forceFlush() { return Promise.resolve(); }
}
```

Users who control the downstream collector can also filter the attribute at the collector pipeline level.
1241254.title: Multiple @opentelemetry/instrumentation-* packages expose database username via unconditional db.user span attribute

1244623.overview:
minimatch 10.2.6 contains an attacker-controlled pattern amplification in firstPhasePreProcess() when optimizationLevel >= 2.

researcher: Reid Downing (b1nv0id)
files: 

- src/index.ts: 690-770
- src/index.ts: 780-796

issue:
input-controlled growth of globParts during first-phase preprocessing, followed by quadratic second-phase processing.

the **/../ transformation clones a globparts entry and appends the clone to the same globparts array:
```
parts.splice(gs, 1)
const other = parts.slice(0)
other[gs] = '**'
globParts.push(other)
```
this occurs inside a do...while (didSomething) fixpoint loop, allowing generated entries to be processed again.

the expanded globparts array is subsequently processed by secondPhasePreProcess(), which performs pairwise comparisons:
```
for (let i = 0; i < globParts.length - 1; i++) {
  for (let j = i + 1; j < globParts.length; j++) {
    this.partsMatch(...)
  }
}
```
an attacker who can supply a glob pattern can therefore cause additional pattern entries to be generated during preprocessing, followed by quadratic pairwise processing, resulting in excessive cpu and memory consumption.
1244623.title: minimatch has potential denial of service via globparts amplification

1246029.overview:
### Summary

With the non-default stopNodes option, a stop node's body with many "<a " fragments and no closing ">" anywhere after makes readStopNodeData() rescan the entire remaining input from every "<". The failed lookahead is neither cached nor bounded, so n fragments cost O(n²) before the parser throws. Availability-only (CPU exhaustion), needs the non-default stopNodes option — not benchmarked yet, see Proof of Concept.

### Details

**CWE-407** — Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity

**Code**
- `OrderedObjParser.js:520` — `parseXml()` calls `readStopNodeData()` after a matching stop node opens
- `OrderedObjParser.js:810` — calls `readTagExp()` for every non-special `<`
- `OrderedObjParser.js:688-722` — `tagExpWithClosingIndex()` scans to end-of-input and returns `undefined` when no `>` exists
- `OrderedObjParser.js:812-818` — on failure, `i` isn't advanced, so the next `<` repeats the same full scan
- `OrderedObjParser.js:423` — the main parse loop throws immediately on the same failure; only the stop-node path retries

**Root cause:** a failed closing-`>` lookahead is neither cached nor bounded — `n` copies of `<a ` with no later `>` means `n` scans over the remaining input, O(n²) work, before it finally throws.

**Fix**
1. Throw immediately in `readStopNodeData()` when `readTagExp()` returns `undefined`
2. Or break the loop on the first failed scan
3. Or find the next `>` once and reuse/bound that result
4. Add a test asserting near-linear scaling when payload size doubles

### Proof of concept

Not benchmarked — static-analysis finding, confidence 0.5.

To confirm: configure `stopNodes` matching a root element. Build input as `'<stop>' + '<a '.repeat(n)`. Time `parse()` until it throws `Unexpected end of <tag>`. Start around n=10,000 and double it — quadratic should show ~4x time per doubling, linear ~2x. Control: same input with a `>` present, or `stopNodes` unset.

### Impact

CPU-exhaustion DoS in Node.js services parsing untrusted XML with `stopNodes` enabled. A ~100KB payload is estimated at ~10⁹ character operations (roughly a second or more of blocked event loop) — analytical estimate, not a benchmark. No confidentiality/integrity impact. CVSS 3.1: `AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` (3.7, Low).
1246029.title: fast-xml-parser: Quadratic CPU consumption scanning unterminated stop-node tags

1246705.overview:
### Summary

`@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` redacts sensitive URL query parameters on **outgoing (client) spans** but not on **incoming (server) spans**. The server-span path writes the raw query string verbatim into the `url.query` attribute, so credentials embedded in inbound request URLs — AWS presigned-URL signatures, Azure SAS tokens (`sig`), GCS signed-URL signatures — are exported in plaintext to the configured tracing backend.

Configuring the `redactedQueryParams` option **does not change this**, as this applies only to outgoing (client) spans.

### Impact

**Information disclosure / credential leakage** (CWE-200; CWE-532, insertion of sensitive information into telemetry data).

**Who is impacted:** any Node.js service instrumented with `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` — directly or transitively via `@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node` — that receives inbound requests carrying credentials in the query string. Common cases: services fronting presigned S3/GCS downloads, Azure SAS-token URLs, and signature-authenticated webhooks.

**Consequence:** clients' still-valid credentials are written into server spans and stored by the tracing backend, readable by anyone with span-read access — observability vendor infrastructure, dashboard users, and internal audiences far broader than the credential's intended scope. Presigned-URL signatures typically remain valid for minutes to days after capture, so this is not merely historical exposure.

**Severity:** Moderate. Exploitation requires read access to the telemetry backend, and inbound URLs must actually carry signed credentials. However, the gap is a documented mitigation that silently fails to apply, which defeats the mitigation operators would reach for.

### Patches

This vulnerability has been patched in `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` version `0.222.0`.
Known sensitive query string values (as defined by Semantic Conventions) are redacted by default from span data for incoming spans.
The `redactedQueryParamsServer` configuration option was added for customization.
1246705.title: OpenTelemetry JavaScript: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File and Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor in @opentelemetry/instrumentation-http

1247486.overview:
Next.js applications with `'use cache'` can disclose cached data across root params when the same `'use cache'` function is called both directly during rendering and through `unstable_cache()`, and that function reads a root param. Root params are route parameters of the root layout, and applications commonly use them to scope data, for example per locale.

During a cold process start, a cross-request deduplication race allowed an `unstable_cache()` call to join the in-flight fill of a concurrent direct call and receive its result, bypassing the root param check that would normally reject it. `unstable_cache()` then stored that result under a cache key without root params, so subsequent requests for other root param values received the same entry until it is revalidated or evicted. Cached data produced for one root param value is returned to requests for other values.

Exploitation requires the `unstable_cache()` request to arrive while the function's first fill after a process start is still in flight. Outside this race, the nesting already throws an error: `'use cache' inside unstable_cache() is unsupported`, and avoiding it is a complete workaround.
1247486.title: Next.js: Information disclosure across root params when a 'use cache' function is called through unstable_cache()

1247710.overview: Picomatch through 4.0.7 contains a regular expression denial of service vulnerability that allows attackers to block the event loop by supplying single-branch repeated extglob patterns. Attackers can provide globs like +(*) or +(*a), which analyzeRepeatedExtglob in lib/parse.js skips, causing exponential backtracking against short crafted strings and denying service to Node.js applications.
1247710.title: picomatch vulnerable to ReDoS through single-branch repeated extglobs

1247712.overview:
With Cache Components enabled, an outer `'use cache'` function can be keyed incorrectly even when its inner `'use cache'` call generates a fresh entry. If the inner function reads a root param (via `next/root-params`) and returns a value that still contains pending promises — for example an object with data that is ready immediately alongside slower data — React Flight delivers the ready portion to the outer function before the inner entry has finished publishing its root param dependencies. The outer function can then finish, and its cache entry is persisted under a key that omits that root param. The entry is written once and reused for all root param values, so a response for one root param value can serve content produced for a different value. Entries written this way can also ignore tag invalidation and cache lifetimes of the nested caches they consumed.

What values are leaked cannot be attacker controlled. Which value's content is served depends only on which invocation wrote the entry first.

This is a variant of https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h694-7cp9-m8p3 that the fix for that advisory does not cover: it does not require the inner call to be served from an existing entry, and it does not depend on a slow cache handler.
1247712.title: Next.js: Cache leak across root param values in nested 'use cache' functions via delayed inner stream metadata
